title: the Shiva Purana (selections)
hook: Brahma and Vishnu are arguing about which of them is greater when a pillar of fire splits the sky between them

segments.voice: Yesterday closed Navaratri as a nine-night curriculum, and the goddess's part of the year, with tools resting under flowers. Today the year turns to Shiva.

Two gods are arguing. Brahma, the creator, says he's the greatest, since everything came from him. Vishnu, the preserver, says no, he is, since he keeps everything going. The argument gets hot. Then, between the two of them, a pillar of fire appears, blazing, going up past where they can see and down past where they can see. No top in sight, and no bottom. Both gods stop mid-sentence. You heard this on Shivaratri, back on day ninety; today it comes from the Shiva Purana itself.
screen: `TWO GODS ARGUING.` → `A PILLAR OF FIRE.` → `NO TOP, NO BOTTOM.`

segments.voice: The Shiva Purana is a big book of stories about Shiva, his worship and the people around him. It presents itself as told aloud: a storyteller named Suta recounting it to a gathering of sages. The path takes selections, not the whole. The two gods agree on a test: whoever finds the end of this thing wins. Vishnu becomes a boar and digs down. Brahma becomes a swan and flies up. They go a very long way. Vishnu finds no bottom, and finally comes back and says so: he couldn't find the end. Brahma finds no top. But on the way he meets a ketaki flower drifting down, and he has an idea. He comes back, says he reached the top, and brings the flower along to swear it's true. Then the pillar opens and Shiva steps out of it. He honors Vishnu for telling the truth and rebukes Brahma for the lie, and in the story the ketaki flower, the false witness, is not to be offered in Shiva's worship. Here's what makes it worth carrying. The point isn't who won. Nobody found the end. For Shaiva devotees, the linga in a Shiva temple recalls this pillar: something that can't be measured from either side. And the one who comes out well is the one who admitted it: I couldn't find the end. Before something that big, the story honors the honest answer, and rebukes the one who pretended to have it figured out.
screen: `A BOOK OF SHIVA'S STORIES.` · `A BOAR DIGS, A SWAN FLIES.` · `ONE ADMITS IT, ONE LIES.` · `A PILLAR NO ONE CAN MEASURE.` · then, large: `I COULDN'T FIND THE END.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one big question you have no answer to, where something comes from, what happens to someone you love, why things are the way they are, and let it stand in front of you like the pillar, too big to measure, without reaching for its top or its bottom. Let any quick answer drift by, like the flower. If you pray, you can say Shiva's name, or the name of God you use, and leave the question with it.
The Shiva Purana. A book of Shiva's stories, told by Suta to the sages.
Your line: the Shiva Purana, in selections. Nobody found the end, and the honest one said so. I'll be here tomorrow.

howItsDone: Shaiva Hindus worship Shiva in the form of the linga in temples and homes, and the story of the endless pillar of fire is told and carved in temples as the appearance of the linga, Lingodbhava; it is also linked to Maha Shivaratri.

notes: First day of the Shiva part (1118–1124 are the Shiva Purana selections). This writer's selections: 1118 the pillar of fire (Vidyeshvara Samhita); 1119 Sati and Daksha's sacrifice; 1120 Kama burned; 1121 Parvati's tapas and the disguised visitor (all Rudra Samhita). 1122–1124 belong to another writer.

Pillar story details: the quarrel over greatness, the fiery column, Vishnu as boar digging down, Brahma as swan flying up, the ketaki flower as false witness, Shiva emerging, Vishnu honored, Brahma rebuked, ketaki excluded from Shiva's worship. Paraphrased; confirm against the Vidyeshvara Samhita. The Bhairava episode (Brahma's fifth head) is omitted.
'Like other Puranas, it presents itself as told aloud by Suta to sages': confirm the frame for the Shiva Purana.
Linga 'recalls' the pillar is offered as the story's own link; Shaiva theologies of the linga vary. Confirm phrasing; the link to Maha Shivaratri appears only in howItsDone.
Original note glosses Purana as 'a book of old stories'; confirm.
